stories.headline: Trump Says He Will 'Veto Everything' if Democrats Win Congressional Control
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump said Friday that he would veto every piece of legislation sent to him during the second half of his term if Democrats win control of the House or Senate in next month's midterm elections. Speaking to reporters on the South Lawn, he said, "Well, I think the Republicans are going to win. But if there was, you call it gridlock, what happens is I veto everything."

Trump added that Democrats would then "come and they want to make a deal. So we'll work it out." The remarks were covered by roughly 15 outlets across the political spectrum and come as both parties make their closing arguments with the election days away.

Supporters of the president see the comment as a statement of negotiating leverage and a warning to voters about what a divided Congress would mean for his agenda. Democrats and critics have framed it as a threat to block governing altogether, arguing that it shows a refusal to work with an opposition-led chamber. Either chamber changing hands would give Democrats subpoena power and control over committee agendas, even if vetoed bills could not become law without two-thirds majorities in both chambers.

The statement follows other late-campaign pledges, including Trump's proposal for a $5,000 dividend payment to Americans if Republicans retain Congress, which has drawn skepticism from fiscal hawks over its estimated $1.3 trillion cost. The midterm elections take place in November.

stories.headline: DOJ Demands California Counties Identify and Sequester Ballots From Suspected Noncitizens
stories.summary:
The Justice Department on Friday sent letters to election officials in every California county asking them to identify potential noncitizens on their voter rolls, according to a letter obtained by NBC News and reports by several outlets. The letters warned that officials who fail to cooperate "risk significant federal scrutiny," as reported by The New York Times.

Federal prosecutors also demanded that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the department said may belong to noncitizens. The department says roughly 20,000 noncitizens received mail-in ballots in California and is asking the state to sequester those votes before they are processed.

The administration and its supporters argue that ensuring only eligible citizens vote is a basic obligation and that federal oversight is warranted. Critics, including many Democrats and election-law advocates, have raised concerns that such demands so close to an election could disrupt ballot processing, lead to eligible voters being flagged in error, and represent federal overreach into state-run elections. The department has not publicly detailed how it arrived at the 20,000 figure.

The letters come amid a wider federal push on election disputes in the run-up to the midterms. Whether California counties comply or challenge the demand in court is the next question to watch, with ballot processing already under way.

stories.headline: Serbia Votes in Tight Parliamentary Election as Student List Challenges Vučić
stories.summary:
Serbians vote Sunday in snap parliamentary elections widely seen as the most serious challenge to President Aleksandar Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party since it entered government in 2012. Analysts predict an extremely tight race, though reliable polling is limited.

The main challenger is the Student List, which emerged from nearly two years of anti-corruption protests sparked by the deaths of 16 people when a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad. Student-led assemblies chose 250 candidates with no political background, headed by cardiologist and Novi Sad University professor Ilija Srdanovic. The movement has no formal hierarchy, and Srdanovic is not its leader.

Vučić stood down as president last month when he called the vote, and is running to become prime minister. He retains strong support among voters who view him as a defender of Serbian interests and credit him with economic growth and infrastructure improvements. He has portrayed the student movement as foreign-backed and aimed at bringing down the state, while Srdanovic says the list offers "the core values of civilised society."

The outcome could determine whether Vučić's long dominance, supported by a largely uncritical media, continues or faces its first real electoral test.

stories.headline: Fire Engulfs Hitler's Eagle's Nest Retreat in Bavaria; Suspect Detained
stories.summary:
Police in Bavaria detained a suspect during a fire at the Kehlsteinhaus, Adolf Hitler's Alpine retreat known as the Eagle's Nest, above the town of Berchtesgaden. Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm at 21:15 local time Friday and firefighters found the building engulfed in flames.

Difficult mountain terrain hampered firefighting, and the blaze was still burning early Saturday with about 200 emergency personnel deployed. No injuries were reported. Police said a criminal investigation is under way to determine whether the suspect is connected to the fire.

Completed in 1938 at about 1,800 metres, the building survived the Nazis' defeat in 1945 and became a tourist destination housing a mountain inn. It sits near the Berghof, where Hitler and top officials planned the 1941 invasion of the USSR.

The fire comes amid ongoing debate in Germany and Austria over whether to preserve, repurpose or demolish Hitler-linked sites. Berlin authorities announced in June they would tear down one of his bunkers, and Austria converted his birthplace into a police station in July. Supporters of preservation cite historical value, while others worry such sites draw neo-Nazi pilgrims.

stories.headline: Update: Supreme Court Rulings Reshape Midterm Landscape as Justice Department Presses Election Disputes
stories.summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way on Thursday for New Hampshire to fully bar the use of student IDs as voter identification in the November midterm elections, warning of voter confusion too close to an election. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, the court's most junior liberal, publicly dissented, writing that she would have left in place a lower court decision. Separately, the court earlier this week temporarily reinstated a federal rule allowing the abortion pill to be prescribed through telemedicine and dispensed by mail, lifting a lower-court order that had narrowed access nationwide.

The Justice Department also escalated election-related actions on Friday. Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California demanding that officials set aside and verify ballots the department says may belong to noncitizens. The DOJ puts the number at roughly 20,000 people who received mail-in ballots, and the letters warn that officials who do not comply "risk significant federal scrutiny." The administration has described the effort as protecting election integrity, while California officials and Democrats call it an escalation in a broader legal fight with the president and an attempt to intimidate local election workers.

In Alaska, President Trump said he directed the Justice Department to sue to block certification of the Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola, citing possible voter confusion because another candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan, is on the ballot. Republicans say the second candidate was placed there to confuse voters, while Peltola called the suit "frivolous" and "clearly corruption." Election law experts have called the lawsuit highly unusual, and one analysis noted no obvious legal authority supports a pre-emptive block on certification. Attorney General Todd Blanche declined to rule out DOJ intervention in certification.

A New York Times/Siena poll found half of respondents were worried Republicans might use illegal means to overturn the midterm results. Early voting is surging in battleground states, including North Carolina, where more than 1.2 million ballots have been accepted, up 37 percent from 2022. Control of Congress is at stake on Nov. 3.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Intelligence Memo Warns of Advanced Iranian Plots to Kill American Officials Abroad
stories.summary:
U.S. intelligence has found that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target American diplomats and officials in the Middle East and beyond, with lethal plots reaching "advanced stages," according to an Oct. 23 memo to Secretary of State Marco Rubio obtained by Axios. The memo was sent by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.

U.S. officials say the intelligence is one reason the State Department is drawing down personnel at several American embassies across the region. The government has ordered diplomats and other federal employees to leave Saudi Arabia, days after a Houthi attack on an airport in the country's east killed two people. Officials cite mounting fears of a broader regional conflict.

The warning comes as the Iran war continues to push oil prices to their highest level since May, and as Iran has issued a "serious warning" to U.S. forces. Reports have also said the United States and Israel have drawn up plans to renew strikes on Iran after the midterm elections, though the White House says no attack will occur before the vote.

The memo adds a new, concrete security dimension to the conflict, bearing on the safety of U.S. personnel abroad and on whether the war widens in the coming weeks. Further embassy drawdowns or retaliatory steps could follow.

stories.headline: Kenya Records Second Ebola Death in First Outbreak as Regional Alarm Grows
stories.summary:
Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first-ever outbreak of the disease. A 65-year-old woman, a close family member of the first victim, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said. She developed symptoms on Oct. 13.

The first victim, a man who had traveled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died in Nairobi on Oct. 5 after being treated at several hospitals. Seven other patients are being treated at two isolation facilities, including three relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner. The ministry says all cases belong to one cluster with no evidence of community spread.

More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making this the second deadliest outbreak on record, with more than 9,500 cases in Congo. The Bundibugyo species involved has no approved vaccine or treatment, though trials are under way. The U.S. has warned citizens against travel to Kenya, and Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are on alert.

Kenya has introduced enhanced screening for travelers from Congo and nine other high-risk countries, requiring a digital surveillance form and QR code, and has ordered enhanced screening of arriving aircraft. The International Rescue Committee says Kenya faces a steady risk of imported cases.

stories.headline: Update: France Deploys 70,000 Officers and Closes Louvre as Nationwide Protests Continue
stories.summary:
French authorities announced the deployment of 70,000 law enforcement officers nationwide to prevent violence during planned protests on Saturday. The Louvre and other museums are closing for the day, and officials have banned demonstrations in several cities, including Marseille and Lyon, drawing criticism from rights groups.

The protests began weeks ago over the poor state of high schools and have grown into broader anger over the cost of living, drawing hundreds of thousands of mostly young people. Last week about 3,000 shops were damaged or looted. The most prominent image was the fire at Limoges city hall, where its wooden clock tower collapsed. Two men, aged 66 and 34, have been arrested, and prosecutors say they have links to "radical-left networks."

Limoges Mayor Guillaume Guérin blames the hard left and rioters, while some young protesters say the building matters less than people living in poverty. Limoges has imposed overnight curfews and limited gatherings in its center to 10 people, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu visited the city on Friday.

The unrest comes against a large fiscal deficit and a centrist government lacking a National Assembly majority, with presidential elections about six months away. Unrest has also spread to cities elsewhere in Europe, including Lisbon, Madrid, Milan and Brussels.
